title: Zscaler Grows as Fast as CrowdStrike at a Fifth of the Multiple
subtitle: Every enterprise vendor promises consolidation, but Wall Street is grading who sells software and who sells discounts.
summary: Zscaler matches rival top-line growth rates at nearly identical gross margins, yet trades at a steep valuation discount across cybersecurity. The split exposes a quiet reckoning over platform economics: whether multi-product bundles drive durable software expansion or merely mask subsidized land-grabs.

keyTerms.definition: A security model that trusts nothing by default. Instead of assuming everything inside the corporate network is safe, every user, device and workload is verified each time it reaches for an application.

A vendor’s campaign to replace several single-purpose security tools with one integrated suite. The prize is a bigger contract; the cost is often a discount, free product during a rival’s remaining term, or payment terms stretched over years.

The revenue a cohort of existing customers pays this year versus last, including upgrades and cancellations. Above 100% means the installed base grows on its own; the rate is the cleanest read on whether a bundle is actually being used or merely tolerated.

The annualised value of subscription contracts in force. It is the number software investors watch instead of quarterly revenue because it moves more smoothly and shows whether new business is keeping up with the base.

When a customer signs a multi-year deal but pays annually rather than up front. The contract value is unchanged on paper, yet the vendor waits longer for cash, so the same booking produces less money sooner.

A credential issued to something that is not a person: a server, a container, or increasingly an AI agent. Each one needs permissions and an audit trail, which is why security pricing is drifting away from a per-employee model.

bottomLine: Consolidation in security is real, but the multiple investors pay for the word “platform” is a bet on expansion quality, not on the pitch. The market has already started grading it: Zscaler and CrowdStrike grow trailing revenue at almost the same rate, yet one trades near nine times sales and the other near forty-two. The difference is whether the modules a customer buys keep selling themselves after year one. Palo Alto Networks has been candid that winning the switch costs something — free product, deferred billing, and a growth trough it has already paid for in a single brutal session. For Zscaler the honest test is its own guidance: mid-teens ARR growth with flat margins, and retention of 115% against above 120% for the best platformised peer. If retention and flexible-commitment value hold while growth re-accelerates, the discount is the mispricing. If they sag, the bundle was bought, not sold.
bodyHtml:
Think of modern enterprise software like a gym trying to bundle smoothies, physical therapy, and personal training onto a single monthly pass. Every cybersecurity vendor now pitches “the platform.” For a corporate tech buyer, the pitch is irresistible. Fire a dozen fragmented vendors, ditch the disconnected tools, and manage everything through one console. The consolidation wave is real, but Wall Street has stopped taking the headline at face value. Instead, the market is quietly grading the quality of that consolidation, and the pricing spread between peers is staggering.

Zscaler acts as an airport security checkpoint built entirely in the cloud. Instead of letting an employee’s laptop connect directly to the public internet or private company apps, every click, login, and downloaded file routes through Zscaler’s inspection engines first. Nothing is trusted simply because it sits inside the corporate network; every packet is checked in real time. Roughly 11,000 customers—including more than 40% of the Forbes Global 2000—pay Zscaler to run this digital checkpoint.

Look at the equity and you immediately hit a puzzle. Zscaler grew fiscal 2026 revenue 25% to $3.35 billion. CrowdStrike expanded trailing revenue at an almost identical 25.8% rate, with near-identical gross margins.

Same growth. Same margin. Yet CrowdStrike commands a valuation multiple near 42 times sales, while Zscaler trades near nine times. A near-fivefold multiple gap on identical growth rates means investors are not paying for top-line speed. They are paying for expansion quality: whether a vendor’s software modules keep selling themselves after the customer signs the initial contract.

That valuation gap traces straight back to the plumbing of platform land-grabs. To win these enterprise consolidations, vendors often subsidize the switch. Palo Alto Networks showed the price of that switch when management acknowledged handing over free product for the remainder of a competitor’s contract. Over six years it has also moved annual billings from about 6% of bookings to roughly 30%, a shift it calls structural. Paying later is a discount in everything but name.

That land-grab triggered a 12-to-18-month growth trough that wiped 28% off its equity in a single 2024 session. The test for any platform vendor is whether the extra modules eventually pay for the discount, or whether the discount was the product all along.

This dynamic matters for the stock because artificial intelligence is fundamentally breaking seat-based pricing. Security software traditionally billed per human worker. But human headcount grows slowly, while autonomous software agents multiply overnight. In a Palo Alto vendor survey, enterprises reported 109 machine identities for every human employee. Independent estimates from Veza put the ratio at 17 to one. OWASP baselines sit near 100 to one.

This measurement chaos is the commercial opportunity. Each agent requires an identity, a permission set, and a real-time audit trail. Zscaler’s ThreatLabz analyzed 989.3 billion AI transactions across roughly 9,000 organizations, with activity climbing 83% year over year. Zscaler is capturing that shift through metered, non-seat usage, which already drives roughly 30% of new and upsell contract value.

To capture that spend, Zscaler rolled out Z-Flex, a flexible commitment structure that logged over $1.7 billion in contract value during fiscal 2026. It lets clients swap modules without a new procurement cycle, and management says customers using it saw an average 30% ARR uplift. Customers running its three-product bundle rose to more than 950 from over 350 a year earlier. But flexible terms can also become a double-edged sword when renewal budgets tighten.

The short thesis begins with Zscaler’s own fiscal 2027 guidance: ARR growth decelerating to between 16.6% and 17.4%, down from 25% in fiscal 2026. Strip out the $141 million in ARR acquired through its $651.4 million Red Canary buyout, and organic ARR growth already cooled to 20%. Meanwhile, net revenue retention sat at 115%, trailing Palo Alto’s platformized cohort at over 120% and Rubrik at over 119%. A 115% retention rate during a platform roll-out suggests customers are digesting discounted bundles rather than buying incremental capacity. Rubrik already flashed this early-warning signal, seeing retention slip below 120% as customer growth above $100,000 cooled and gross margins dipped 60 basis points.

Microsoft bundles security into the enterprise software companies already buy. Palo Alto is absorbing lower gross margins on cloud hosting. Zscaler risks margin compression at the top and pricing resistance at the bottom.

What we are watching is whether Zscaler can re-accelerate ARR growth back above 20% while holding retention at 115% or better. What proves the bears wrong is evidence that clients are paying full freight for modular expansion rather than trading down on flexible terms. For the equity to re-rate from its discount multiple, Zscaler has to prove its platform creates pricing leverage instead of just hiding a pricing concession.
